title: Classification, Sex, and Eligibility
bigQuestion: When a sports body sorts athletes into categories, whose evidence decides which box a person belongs in, and who can challenge it?

story.title: A Box on a Form
story.kicker: Every entry form asks an athlete to fit a category, and the category was written by a governing body.
paragraphs: An entry form for an international track meet asks for a name, a nation, an event and a category. The category line looks simple. Yet the words behind it, women's or men's, open or classified, were written by a governing body. Those bodies have rewritten them many times since the 1920s.

Some categories exist to open doors. Women's events were added to the Olympic track program in 1928 only after women organized their own games. Paralympic classes exist so that athletes with different impairments can compete against others with similar ones. Without those boxes, many athletes would have had no place to enter at all.

Every box also has an edge, and someone has to decide who stands on which side. Since 1966, track officials have used physical inspections, chromosome tests and hormone limits to police the women's category. Paralympic officials have used medical files and observation. Each method has been challenged, and several have been dropped.

This chapter follows those rules as institutions. It asks who wrote each rule, what evidence it used, which athletes it shut out or let in, and which court or panel heard the appeal. The goal is to describe a live argument accurately, with names and dates, not to settle it with a slogan.
story.think: Why might a category that opens a door for one group of athletes also create a new question about who belongs inside it?

lessons.title: Women at the Early Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Women entered the modern Olympics in 1900, but the IOC kept them out of track and field until 1928.
reading: The first modern Olympics, in Athens in 1896, had no events for women. Pierre de Coubertin, the French founder of the *International Olympic Committee* (IOC), opposed women competing in public. At the 1900 Paris Games women entered a few sports, including tennis and golf. Charlotte Cooper of Britain won the tennis singles and became the first woman to win an Olympic event.

Track and field, the center of the Games, stayed closed to women for three more decades. The sport's world body, the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), was founded in 1912 and ran only men's events at first. Swimming added women's races in 1912 in Stockholm. Each federation decided on its own whether women had a *category* in its sport.

Women's track events finally appeared at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, with five events. After the 800 meters, newspapers claimed that runners had collapsed, and officials dropped the race. Women did not run an Olympic 800 meters again until 1960 in Rome. The story shows how a category could be opened and closed by the same officials within one Games.

words.d: the body founded in 1894 that runs the Olympic Games and decides which sports and events they include
a group, such as women's or men's, that a sports body sets up so that only certain athletes compete against each other
the world governing body for one sport, which writes that sport's rules and entry standards

lessons.title: Milliat's Women's Games
lessons.mainIdea: When the IOC refused women's track events, Alice Milliat built a separate women's federation and its own world games.
reading: Alice Milliat was a French rower and sports organizer. In 1919 she asked the IOC to add women's track and field to the 1920 Games, and it refused. In 1921 she and others founded the *Fédération Sportive Féminine Internationale* (FSFI), an international federation run for women's sport. It set its own records and rules.

In August 1922 the FSFI held the first *Women's World Games* in Paris. Athletes from five nations, including the United States and Britain, competed before a large crowd in a single day. More Women's World Games followed in Gothenburg in 1926, Prague in 1930 and London in 1934. The IAAF objected at first to the FSFI using the word Olympic.

The separate games put pressure on the IAAF and IOC. A rival body with its own records threatened their control of the sport. The IAAF agreed to a small women's program for 1928, and by the mid-1930s it took over women's records. The FSFI then faded and dissolved. The case shows a shut-out group building a *parallel* institution to force a door open.

words.d: the international women's sports federation founded in 1921 by Alice Milliat and others
international women's track meets held by the FSFI from 1922 to 1934
running side by side, as a separate institution built by people shut out of an older one

look.title: Two Bodies, One Sport
look.text: In 1922 two bodies claim to govern women's running. The IAAF, run by men, has no women's events. The FSFI, led by Alice Milliat, has women's events, women's records and a world meet in Paris. Newspapers print times from the FSFI meet beside men's records from the IAAF.
look.prompt: Why would the IAAF want to take over women's records once the FSFI had them? What did Milliat gain and lose when that happened?

check.q: What did Alice Milliat do after the IOC refused women's track events?
check.why: In 1921 she helped found the FSFI, which ran women's track meets.

check.q: Where were the first Women's World Games held in 1922?
check.why: The FSFI held the first Women's World Games in Paris in August 1922.

check.q: What does parallel mean in this lesson?
choices: A separate institution built by people shut out
A rule copied from men's sport
A race run on two tracks
check.why: The FSFI was a parallel body, built beside the IAAF because women were shut out.

lessons.title: A Marathon Without Women
lessons.mainIdea: Road races and the Olympics kept women out of the marathon for decades; Boston admitted women in 1972 and the Olympics in 1984.
reading: The Boston Marathon, first run in 1897, had no category for women. In 1966 Roberta Gibb ran it without a number after hiding near the start. In 1967 Kathrine Switzer entered as K. V. Switzer and received an official *bib*, the numbered cloth runners wear. A race official tried to pull her number off during the race, and photographs of the scene spread worldwide.

The Amateur Athletic Union, which then governed American distance running, barred women from races longer than a few miles. Runners and organizers pushed back through the late 1960s. In 1972 the Boston Marathon officially opened a women's division. Nina Kuscsik won it that first year. The rule change came from the race and the national body, not from the runners' fitness.

The IOC added a women's Olympic marathon for the 1984 Los Angeles Games. Joan Benoit of Maine won it. The women's 10,000 meters did not join the Olympics until 1988 in Seoul. These dates show that the women's category grew event by event, each through a vote by a *governing body*.

words.d: the numbered cloth a registered runner wears, proof of an official entry
the body founded in 1888 that governed much of American amateur sport, including road running
an organization that writes the rules and decides who may enter a sport's events

lessons.title: Inspections and Chromosomes
lessons.mainIdea: From 1966 track officials checked women athletes' bodies, and from 1968 the IOC used a chromosome test.
reading: In the Cold War years, some Western officials and newspapers claimed that men were entering women's events. Historians have found little evidence for that claim. Even so, at the 1966 European Championships in Budapest, the IAAF required women to pass a physical inspection by doctors. Many athletes later described the checks as humiliating. The inspections were a new kind of *eligibility* rule.

In 1968 the IOC replaced inspections with a laboratory test. The *Barr body test* looked at cells scraped from inside the cheek for a sign of two X chromosomes. It was used at the Winter Games in Grenoble and the Summer Games in Mexico City. Women who passed received a certificate so they would not need to be tested again.

Geneticists soon pointed out problems. Some women have chromosome patterns that differ from the typical XX, yet their bodies gain no athletic advantage from it. Such natural variations are now often called *differences of sex development* (DSD). A test built on one marker could shut out women who had lived as women their whole lives.

words.d: the rules for who is allowed to enter a competition or category
a chromosome test from cheek cells, used by the IOC to screen women athletes from 1968
natural variations in chromosomes, hormones or anatomy; often shortened to DSD

look.title: A Certificate in a Suitcase
look.text: A woman sprinter arrives at the 1968 Mexico City Games. Before she may race, she gives a cheek sample to a laboratory. If she passes, she receives a card saying she is eligible for women's events. Men's athletes receive no such card, because no one checks who enters the men's category.

check.why: The 1966 European Championships in Budapest used physical inspections.

check.q: What did the Barr body test examine?
choices: Cheek cells for a chromosome marker
check.why: The test looked at cheek cells for a sign of two X chromosomes.

check.q: What problem did geneticists raise about chromosome screening?
choices: It could shut out women with natural variations
check.why: Some women have chromosome differences but no athletic advantage, so a single marker misjudged them.

lessons.title: Martínez-Patiño Appeals
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish hurdler María José Martínez-Patiño challenged a failed chromosome test in 1985 and was reinstated.
reading: María José Martínez-Patiño was a Spanish hurdler. At the 1985 World University Games in Kobe, Japan, she failed the chromosome screen. Tests showed she had a Y chromosome and *androgen insensitivity*, a condition in which the body cannot respond to testosterone. She had lived as a woman all her life and did not know of the condition.

Spanish officials told her to fake an injury and withdraw quietly. She refused. News of the result became public, and she lost her place on the national team, her records and her scholarship. She then worked with geneticist Albert de la Chapelle and others to show that her condition gave her no advantage. In 1988 the IAAF restored her *eligibility*.

Her case helped end universal screening. The IAAF stopped testing every woman in the early 1990s. In 1999 the IOC voted to drop routine sex testing before the 2000 Sydney Games. From then on, officials could still examine an athlete whose eligibility was questioned. That shift moved sex testing from a gate for everyone to a *case-by-case* review.

words.d: a condition in which the body cannot respond to testosterone and related hormones
to restore someone's right to compete after a ban
handled one athlete at a time when a question is raised, instead of testing everyone

look.title: A Hurdler Writes Her Own Record
look.text: Martínez-Patiño wrote that after the failed test she lost friends, her records and her place on the team. She said she felt that her whole identity had been erased overnight, and that she chose to fight in public so other women would not face the same treatment.
look.cite: María José Martínez-Patiño, "Personal Account: A Woman Tried and Tested," The Lancet, December 2005
look.prompt: Why did she refuse to withdraw quietly? What did her public fight change for other athletes?

check.q: What did Spanish officials first tell Martínez-Patiño to do?
check.why: Officials urged her to withdraw quietly by faking an injury, and she refused.

check.q: In what year did the IAAF restore her eligibility?
check.why: After she showed her condition gave no advantage, the IAAF reinstated her in 1988.

check.q: What changed when the IOC dropped routine sex testing before 2000?
choices: All testing was banned by law
check.why: Officials could still review a questioned athlete, but not everyone was screened.

lessons.title: Testosterone Limits and Court
lessons.mainIdea: Since 2011 track's governing body has used testosterone limits for women, and athletes have fought them at CAS and in European courts.
reading: In 2011 the IAAF introduced *hyperandrogenism* rules. Hyperandrogenism means naturally high levels of testosterone. Women above a set limit had to lower their levels to compete. Indian sprinter Dutee Chand was barred under the rules and appealed to the *Court of Arbitration for Sport* (CAS), a tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland, that hears sports disputes.

In July 2015 CAS suspended the IAAF rules. The panel said the IAAF had not shown enough evidence that natural testosterone gave a large advantage. The IAAF then wrote new rules in 2018 that applied only to events from 400 meters to the mile. South African runner Caster Semenya, a two-time Olympic 800 meters champion, challenged them.

In 2019 CAS ruled against Semenya, calling the rules discriminatory but necessary. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court upheld that ruling in 2020. Semenya then took her case to the *European Court of Human Rights*, which ruled in her favor on procedural grounds in July 2023. World Athletics, the IAAF's new name, extended its limits to all women's events that year.

words.d: naturally high levels of testosterone and related hormones
a tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland, founded in 1984, that decides disputes in international sport
a court in Strasbourg, France, that hears claims that a European state violated the European Convention on Human Rights
the name the IAAF adopted in 2019 for track and field's world governing body

lessons.title: Transgender Athlete Policies
lessons.mainIdea: IOC rules for transgender athletes changed in 2004, 2015 and 2021, and each federation now writes its own.
reading: A *transgender* person has a gender identity different from the sex recorded at birth. In 2004 the IOC adopted the Stockholm Consensus. It allowed transgender athletes to compete after surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormone therapy. Few athletes met all three conditions, and critics said the surgery rule had no link to performance.

In November 2015 the IOC issued new guidelines. They dropped the surgery requirement. Transgender women could enter women's events if their testosterone stayed below 10 nanomoles per liter for at least twelve months. The guidelines were advice to federations, not binding rules, and federations applied them in different ways.

In November 2021 the IOC published its *Framework on Fairness, Inclusion and Non-Discrimination*. It said no athlete should be presumed to have an advantage and handed eligibility decisions to each sport's federation. In 2023 World Athletics barred transgender women who had gone through male puberty from the women's category. Swimming's federation had adopted a similar rule in 2022, so rules now differ from sport to sport.

words.d: having a gender identity different from the sex recorded at birth
the IOC's 2004 rules for transgender athletes, which required surgery, legal recognition and hormone therapy
a set of principles that guides rule makers without writing every rule itself

look.title: Three IOC Documents
look.text: 2004: an athlete may compete after surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormones. 2015: surgery is no longer required; testosterone must stay below a set level for twelve months. 2021: the IOC sets principles, and each federation writes its own eligibility rules based on evidence from its sport.
look.prompt: Who held the decision in 2004, and who held it after 2021? Why might a sport-by-sport approach lead to different rules for swimming and track?

check.q: What did the 2004 Stockholm Consensus require that the 2015 guidelines dropped?
check.why: The 2015 guidelines dropped the surgery requirement of the Stockholm Consensus.

check.q: What did the IOC's 2021 framework do with eligibility decisions?
choices: Handed them to each sport's federation
Kept one rule for every sport
check.why: The framework set principles and left the rules to each federation.

check.q: Why do rules for transgender athletes now differ between sports?
choices: They are set by the United Nations
Each federation writes its own policy
check.why: Since 2021 each federation, such as World Athletics or swimming's body, writes its own policy.

lessons.title: Sydney 2000 and a Ban
lessons.mainIdea: After a Spanish team broke eligibility rules at Sydney 2000, the IPC removed athletes with intellectual impairments until 2012.
reading: At the 2000 Sydney Paralympics, Spain won the gold medal in basketball for athletes with an *intellectual impairment*. That term means a significant limit in thinking and learning skills that appears in childhood. Soon after, a Spanish journalist, Carlos Ribagorda, revealed that he had played on the team. He said most of the players had never been tested and had no impairment.

Spain's sports officials investigated and confirmed the fraud. The team returned its medals. The *International Paralympic Committee* (IPC), the world body for the Paralympics, then suspended all events for athletes with intellectual impairments. It said it needed a reliable way to check eligibility before those athletes could return.

The ban lasted more than a decade and shut out many honest athletes. The IPC worked with the international federation for athletes with intellectual impairments, now called Virtus, to build new tests. Athletes with intellectual impairments returned at the London 2012 Paralympics in three sports: athletics, swimming and table tennis. The case shows how one fraud closed a category for everyone in it.

words.d: a significant limit in thinking and learning skills that begins in childhood
the world governing body for the Paralympic Games, founded in 1989
deliberate cheating by giving false information

lessons.title: Pistorius and the Open Track
lessons.mainIdea: In 2008 CAS overturned a ban on Oscar Pistorius's prosthetic legs, and he ran in the 2012 Olympics.
reading: Oscar Pistorius was a South African sprinter who ran on carbon-fiber *prosthetic* legs, artificial limbs built for running. He won Paralympic gold in 2004. He then tried to qualify for the Olympics against runners without disabilities. In 2007 the IAAF added a rule against devices that give a runner an advantage over one not using them.

In January 2008 the IAAF ruled Pistorius ineligible, citing a study it had paid for. He appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. In May 2008 CAS overturned the ban. The panel said the IAAF had not proven that the prosthetics gave him an overall advantage over a whole race. The ruling put the *burden of proof* on the governing body.

Pistorius ran the 400 meters and the 4 x 400 meters relay at the London 2012 Olympics, the first double-leg amputee to run on an Olympic track. He then raced at the London Paralympics weeks later. In 2013 he killed Reeva Steenkamp at his home, and South African courts later convicted him of her murder. His eligibility case remains a legal precedent even though his name is now tied to that crime.

words.d: an artificial body part, such as a leg, made to replace a missing limb
the duty of one side in a dispute to prove its claim
an earlier decision that later panels and courts look to in similar cases

look.title: Who Must Prove It?
look.text: Rule: a runner may not use a device that gives an advantage. The IAAF says the prosthetics help. The athlete says they help at some points of a race and hurt at others, like the start. The CAS panel must decide which side has to prove its case, and how strong that proof must be.
look.prompt: Why does it matter which side carries the burden of proof? How did that choice decide the Pistorius case?

check.q: Why did CAS overturn the IAAF ban on Pistorius in 2008?
choices: The IAAF had not proven an overall advantage
He switched to a different event
The Olympics had no rules on devices
check.why: CAS said the governing body had not proven the prosthetics gave an overall advantage.

check.q: What does burden of proof mean?
choices: The weight of a prosthetic leg
The fee to file an appeal
The duty of one side to prove its claim
The number of judges on a panel
check.why: Burden of proof is which side must prove its claim in a dispute.

check.q: What did Pistorius do at the London 2012 Olympics?
choices: Ran the 400 meters and the relay
check.why: He ran the 400 meters and the 4 x 400 meters relay.

lessons.title: A Code for Classification
lessons.mainIdea: In 2007 the IPC adopted an Athlete Classification Code so that sorting athletes rests on written rules and research.
reading: Early Paralympic sport sorted athletes by medical diagnosis, such as spinal cord injury or amputation. Each disability group ran its own classes, so one Games could have many small events. In the 1990s the IPC began moving toward *functional classification*. That system groups athletes by how an impairment affects a particular sport, not by the name of the diagnosis.

In November 2007 the IPC General Assembly approved the *IPC Athlete Classification Code*. It set shared rules for all Paralympic sports. It listed which impairments are eligible, required trained classifiers, and gave athletes a right to protest a class. A revised Code took effect in 2015 and called for classification to be *evidence-based*, tied to research on each sport.

Classification disputes still reach the news. Athletes and coaches have argued that some rivals were placed in classes with less severe impairments. Other athletes have lost their eligibility after a review and ended careers. The Code gives these disputes a written process, with protests and appeals, instead of leaving them to a single official's judgment.

words.d: grouping athletes by how an impairment affects a sport, not by medical diagnosis
the IPC's shared classification rules, adopted in 2007 and revised in 2015
built on research data rather than on custom or opinion
in classification, a formal request to review an athlete's class

look.title: What the Code Promises
look.text: The Code states that classification exists to decide who is eligible to compete in Para sport and to group athletes into classes, so that the impact of impairment on the outcome of competition is kept as small as possible.
look.cite: International Paralympic Committee, IPC Athlete Classification Code, 2015
look.prompt: What two jobs does the Code give classification? Why would a written protest process matter to an athlete?

check.q: What is functional classification?
choices: Sorting athletes by medical diagnosis name

check.why: Functional classification groups athletes by the effect of an impairment on a particular sport.

check.q: When did the IPC General Assembly approve the first Athlete Classification Code?
check.why: The first Code was approved in November 2007 and revised in 2015.

check.q: What did the 2015 revision call for?
check.why: The revised Code called for classification tied to research on each sport.
